title: The Least Productive Day of the Year
text:
Kelsey Rogers, a 26-year-old working in construction in San Antonio, Texas, didn’t want to tell her boss why she was asking for time off. First, she chalked it up to “personal reasons.” Then she said her birthday was coming up. But eventually, she came clean: She wanted to play Grand Theft Auto VI right when the game dropped, on November 19. Rogers had big plans—decorating with neon lights, stocking up on energy drinks, adorning those drinks with little paper umbrellas. She and her fiancé were going to play until their eyes gave out.

 She didn’t have to worry: Her boss admitted that he was taking time off for the same reason. “I don’t think the company’s even going to be up and running for probably two or three days,” Rogers told me. If you’ve got a metal roof that needs replacing in south-central Texas, it just might have to wait.

 Rogers and her co-workers will be joined by an untold number of other players who have rearranged their lives, in ways large and small, so they can savor their first taste of this particular game. The Grand Theft Auto series, which debuted in 1997, is one of the most lucrative and influential franchises in video-game history. Each installment has expanded the technical possibilities of the medium: the density of graphical detail, the players’ freedom to roam the world, the game’s responsiveness to players’ actions. (Each has also drawn controversy: In GTA IV , players could drive drunk; GTA: San Andreas contained hidden code for an interactive, sexually explicit cutscene.) Fans have been waiting for GTA VI , in which they play petty criminals ascending an urban underworld, since the previous release by Rockstar Games 13 years ago. They don’t want to risk being left behind on launch day.

 [ Read: What Lego lost when it grew up ] 

 The release of GTA VI, which has already raked in $1 billion in presales , may briefly warp the economy; one survey estimated that some 12.5 million adults will alter their work or school schedules to play. The launch will also have ripple effects on people’s sense of social obligations. One software engineer in New York told me that she’d volunteered to work through Thanksgiving so she could guarantee time off for GTA ; she’d warned loved ones not to worry if she didn’t answer texts. A program analyst I spoke with plans to lug her console on the Amtrak ride to visit her girlfriend for their first anniversary, which falls on the 19th. “You have me all evening,” she told her partner; the daytime would be for Cheetos and couchside carjacking. (Some interviewees, who were concerned about their employers finding out about their activities, requested not to be identified with their full name.) Kane Webb, a freelance sportswriter in Bakersfield, California, will be celebrating his tenth wedding anniversary. He and his wife had contemplated a trip to Disneyland, but once Rockstar confirmed the launch, “there really wasn’t any question of what we were going to do that day,” Webb told me. He’ll have to skip covering the end of tennis season; to make up the lost income, the couple will pick up delivery gigs at Walmart.

 Some employers have surrendered to the hype: Logitech declared a new floating holiday for gaming—which did not have to be used on Grand Theft Auto , Amanda Glasgow, the company’s chief communications officer, hastened to tell me. (One office in the company’s gaming division will host a special “streaming event” on November 19, however.) Not even the armed forces are immune. The 9th Engineer Battalion, based in Fort Stewart, Georgia, rolled out a reenlistment incentive aligning with the GTA VI release: By signing up by November 14 and committing to at least two years of additional service, soldiers could get a four-day time-off pass for the weekend—a guaranteed 96-hour virtual crime spree. Forty-three soldiers took the Army up on it—“a pretty big number,” Staff Sergeant Brittany Wolfer, the battalion’s career counselor, told me. Although Wolfer, a gamer herself, had first floated the idea jokingly, she came to see the program as a way to bridge the military’s generational gap. “We were just trying to get the soldiers’ attention, really,” Wolfer said, “and it worked.”

 Of course, pop culture’s history is littered with examples of fevered anticipation: Charles Dickens readers storming a New York wharf, where incoming ships carried the final chapters of The Old Curiosity Shop ; Christopher Nolan diehards crossing the country to see The Odyssey in the best way possible . But the hours it takes to finish even an epic novel or film pale in comparison with the time commitment demanded by today’s big-budget games. The storyline of the most recent Grand Theft Auto entry took about 32 hours to complete; the main quest of GTA VI , according to the developers , should take at least 80. This estimate doesn’t factor in the many hours spent simply exploring, which is what many players will spend most of their time doing. Fans didn’t talk with me much—or at all—about the central narrative, which concerns the escapades of a Bonnie-and-Clyde-like duo in a fictionalized Miami. What really excited them was the prospect of testing the environment, down to the minutiae: ordering a burger, walking the alleys between buildings. “You’re going to be able to listen to the radio outside of the car ,” Jarred Escobedo, a 30-year-old hospital administrator, enthused.

 [ Read: Literature is becoming more like a video game ] 

 Checking out every nook and cranny could easily become a full-time undertaking. For those who have made playing video games their vocation, the enterprise might risk feeling like work. One popular Twitch streamer, Kai Cenat, even felt compelled to warn his followers about his leisurely approach, declaring on X that he wasn’t planning to rush through it: “Giving you guys clarity on GTA 6 I plan to be fully immersed into the game.” Cenat and his fellow professionals are not the only ones aiming to capitalize on the attention that GTA attracts. Korey Batey, a driving instructor in Detroit, told me that he uses Grand Theft Auto to make jokey social-media demos on such topics as road signs and parallel parking. But he’s otherwise not a fan. “Honestly, I hate playing this video game,” he admitted. “So boring.” The videos help drum up business for his school, however, and he can’t risk them going stale—so come November 19, he, too, will fire up the latest installment. His main hope is that the in-game driving has gotten more realistic: “In GTA V , you weren’t able to actually use those outside mirrors.”

 Such dedication makes sense, considering how many players have spent their formative years with this franchise. Rogers, the general contractor, said that she’d started playing San Andreas with her dad at the age of 6, visiting the public library to print out a binder’s worth of cheat codes. At 14, she registered on the online multiplayer extension of GTA V and, as of this writing, has logged 92 days, 15 hours, and 28 minutes of playtime. There, Rogers befriended other kids scattered across Texas and halfway around the planet; one of them was a quiet nerd who, 10 years after they started playing together, proposed marriage on a cruise setting sail out of Los Angeles.

 Still, most people I spoke with could no longer afford the heedless binges of their teen years—physically, financially, interpersonally. Others had project deadlines, bills to pay, toddlers to put to bed; they had bodies approaching middle age that needed a little more exercise and a lot more sleep than they used to. But if they rearrange their obligations just right, they could join in the thrill of this gigantic collective snow day, during which millions will log on and look out onto this virtual world’s untrodden expanse. They will nestle in their chairs and pursue their fictitious lawbreaking, feeling the authentic glee of getting away with something.
